lesson.title: Which Way Does the Evidence Point? The Two-Sided Test
lesson.summary: A two-sided test checks whether a parameter differs from a claimed value in either direction, using an alternative hypothesis written with a not-equal-to sign, and that choice changes how much of the sampling distribution counts as evidence.
lesson.body:
Every hypothesis test starts with a null hypothesis H0, a specific claim about a population parameter, and an alternative hypothesis Ha, the claim you would lean toward if the evidence contradicts H0. Some alternatives point in a single direction, like Ha: mu < 16 or Ha: p > 0.5. A two-sided test, also called two-tailed, instead uses an alternative of the form Ha: mu is not equal to some value. It says only that the parameter is different from the null value, without committing to a direction. You choose two-sided whenever your real question is "did something change," not "did it change in this specific direction."

The choice between one-sided and two-sided is not a technicality, it changes the answer you get. Because Ha: mu is not equal to 16 is satisfied by values both above and below 16, evidence against H0 can come from either tail of the sampling distribution, and a fair test has to count both tails when measuring how surprising a result is.

Here is a concrete case. A cereal company states that its boxes contain a mean of 16 ounces, and years of records show the filling machine produces weights with a standard deviation of 0.3 ounces. A quality control inspector does not know whether the machine has drifted high or low, only that it might have drifted, so she sets up a two-sided test: H0: mu = 16 versus Ha: mu is not equal to 16. She weighs a random sample of 36 boxes and gets a sample mean of 15.9 ounces. Standardizing that gap gives a test statistic of z = (15.9 minus 16) divided by (0.3 divided by the square root of 36), which is negative 0.1 divided by 0.05, or z = negative 2.00. Later chapters will show exactly how to turn that z into a p-value, but the short version is that because this is a two-sided test, both tails count: the two-sided p-value works out to 2 times 0.0228, or 0.0456. If the inspector instead had a specific, pre-existing reason to suspect only underfilling, so that Ha: mu < 16, the p-value would just be the single tail, 0.0228, half as large. Two-sided tests are more conservative for exactly this reason: they spend the suspicion across two possibilities instead of one, which is the honest choice whenever the direction genuinely was not known in advance.

One rule matters more than any formula here: you must decide whether a test is one-sided or two-sided before collecting or looking at the data, based on the real research question. Switching to a one-sided test after peeking at the data, just because the sample happened to land below 16, is a way of manufacturing a smaller p-value that does not reflect honest evidence. Because most real questions in practice are "did anything change" rather than "did it change in one predicted direction," two-sided tests are the more common default, and they should be your starting assumption unless there is a strong, stated reason to expect only one direction.
